newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major flees scandals on rural campaign trail.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major flees scandals on rural campaign trail.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major escaped from London on Thursday, hoping to exchange sensational sleaze and sex stories for a gloriously humdrum slice of village life.

Bury, an anonymous village among the endless flats of Cambridgeshire, could not have been further from the political rough and tumble of the capital -- and Major was clearly glad to be there, even with the London media in tow.

"All around the country, there are communities like this which are concerned with the real events of life and not the dramas you refer to," he said when asked for the umpteenth time about the latest allegations dogging his Conservative party.

As for the "real events" that matter in Bury, villagers turned out in force to see Major open their new village hall, exchange small talk with the local bigwigs and toss a football around with boys in a rare splash of March sun.

Major, who was recently snapped at the wheel of a racing car with no wheels, refused point-blank to join in their cricket practice, no doubt fearing caption writers would refer to his sticky wicket or quickly have him bowled for a duck.
"I'll just watch you," he insisted as impish boy upon impish boy implored him to join them at the nets.
Also present were little girls in lemon dresses, with easter eggs and flower baskets, and a loquacious John Rignall, chairman of Bury Residents Charity and master of ceremonies for the day.
Rignall regaled locals and Londoners alike with the entire history of the village hall, admitting at the outset that he had agonised over just what words to choose.
His words flowed on and on, as he reminded Major of a "little recession" that had once threatened the hall and listed the very many people who had finally made its opening possible.

There was Tanya to thank for the microwave, Barclays Bank for the clock, Alf and his wife for the crockery, Brian who had made the seats and Anglia Water who are "always looked on as bad boys but they waived the infrasctructure charge."

Major and Brian Mawhinney, chairman of the beleagured Conservatives, could barely stifle their giggles at this return to old-fashioned stump politics, more resonant of the easy-going 1950s than the cut-throat 1997 campaign.
"I think, ladies and gentlemen, I have said enough now," Rignall finally said to loud laughs, providing welcome relief in a campaign marked by dark charges and counter charges.
"If anyone in the national press ever wanted to know -- now you know why I love this constituency," Major replied.

He had in fact come to say goodbye -- not because he expects to lose the May 1 election as all the pundits predict -- but because boundary changes have shifted Bury out of his constituency and more gruelling campaigning would soon beckon.

Major admitted he was "a little sad" to be losing Bury but offered more smiles than tears. As for wishes, the most modest of prime ministers aimed lamentably low when asked what he wanted for his 54th birthday on Saturday.
Election Victory? An end to the campaign? World peace? Not a bit of it. "To be 53!" he replied.
